en: (AM 223) Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
That which has conquered this world by its lights, that which is victorious within the earth,
and even that mass of excellences which is the transformation of the truth of the ten syllables of non-duality— [all these belong] to the glories [of Him].
May those wonderful deeds of the wielder of the thunderbolt— who are carried by those whose hearts are moistened by the nectar of supreme compassion— run as a refuge for your own intellects.

May the Vajra-holder, whose conduct is beautiful, swiftly bestow supreme and unfailing glory through the streams of his words fashioned by him, which are adorned with circles of vajra-garlands and highly esteemed.
For here, according to the Blessed One, for one who possesses superior wisdom and has well-cultivated meditative concentration through the gradual stages of weak and medium [faculties],
the yoga— which is endowed with the excellence of all aspects, performs emanation and reabsorption, and is instantly perfected through gnosis— is called "perfected."

For he is resolute in order to lead you and all sentient beings to the state of Vajradhara; ascertaining that the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, are of the nature of a reflection, of a single flavor with emptiness, he enters the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

Instantly, surrounded by his retinue within the interior of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) maṇḍala, adorned by the Lord of the Family (*kuleśa*), joined with the seed-syllable in his heart, consisting of great bliss which is the single flavor of emptiness and compassion, he—taking the form of Śrī Vajrasattva, Mañjuvajra, and others—emanates immeasurable Tathāgatas, goddesses, bodhisattvas, wrathful deities, and so forth.

Performing deeds for the benefit of others according to their capacity through the teaching of the Dharma and other means, establishing the limit of others' merit and withdrawing it as well, he arises with an inconceivable form.
In this regard, the preliminary arrangement and so forth is as follows:

the ground consists of diamond, blazing and composed of a single solid essence, with its expanse extending down to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and bounded by a circle of flame-rays like the fire at the end of an aeon;
from the subterranean realm upwards to the highest heights, it is formed into a single seamless mass above a thick, dense, and blazing diamond wall.

Above is a net of vajra-arrows, below it is adorned with a canopy of vajras, and there is a blazing cage of vajras; within that is a ten-spoked wheel, yellow and rotating clockwise, situated upon a sun disc on a double lotus.
On the eastern spoke therein is Yamāntaka, black, with white and red faces, holding a black vajra-mallet, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the south is Prajñāntaka, white, with black and red faces, holding a white staff marked with a vajra, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.

In the west is Padmāntaka, red, with blue and white faces, holding a red lotus, a sword, a jewel, and a wheel. In the north is Vighnāntaka, black, with white and red faces, holding a fierce vajra, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the southeast is Ṭakkirāja, blue in color, with white and red faces, holding a goad, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the southwest is Nīladaṇḍa, black, with white and red faces, holding a blue staff, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the northwest is Mahābala, black, with white and red faces, holding a trident, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the northeast is Acala, blue in color, with white and red faces, holding a sword, a vajra, a jewel, and a lotus.
Above is Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, yellow, with blue and red faces, holding a yellow wheel, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
Below is Sumbharāja, blue, with white and red faces, bearing a vajra, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
Among them, Uṣṇīṣacakrin, Acala, and Sumbha wear jeweled crowns, possess various precious ornaments, and are graceful; they show their fangs slightly and are clean-shaven.

The others have deformed appearances with knitted brows; their hair, eyebrows, and beards are tawny and erect, their mouths are terrifying with protruding fangs, their tongues loll out, they laugh with loud, boisterous laughter, and they are cruel, adorned with eight serpents, and dwarfed in stature.

Fat and pot-bellied, all ten of these remain motionless upon their seats in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; they stand upon suns situated on slightly touching universal lotuses at the tips of arrows, possessing solar radiance,
wrathful, blazing, roaring, and most terrifying, with faces whose rays resemble the fire of universal destruction.
Through emanations of their own forms in immeasurable bodies, they repeatedly uproot the entire multitude of obstacles throughout the three limitless realms.
Having six arms, they embrace their respective consorts (prajñā) with the two principal arms; they have three faces.
The central face has the same color as the body, while the right and left faces have the colors as previously described; each face possesses three round, red eyes.
And the wheel, due to its extreme rapid rotation, appears as if motionless; it continuously flashes with a multitude of many flames, and within its hub,
above a lower thread and inside a large white triangular *dharmodayā*, upon a universal-petaled lotus situated within the interior of the lower corner, [is the seat].
Accompanied by the universal *viśvavajra*, the directional spokes of that *vajra* are of the same color as Vairocana and the other [Buddhas] as appropriate, as is the altar.

Upon that [altar] is the gabled temple (*kūṭāgāra*), perfected from jewels of five colors, radiant, and pervading the entire circle of directions with the variegated rays of light from the mandala of the Lord of Sages.
In its center is the Blessed One Vajrasattva in the form of Mañjuvajra, saffron-red in hue, with a black face on the right and a white face on the left.

He is embraced by his own consort Prajñā with his two principal arms; he holds a sword, an arrow, a blue lotus, and a bow; he wears a jewel crown and various ornaments of precious gems, and his radiance is infinite.
In the eastern direction is Vairocana, white in color, with black and red faces on his right and left respectively, holding a white eight-spoked wheel, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the southern direction is Ratneśa, yellow in color, holding a nine-faceted emerald gem, a sword, a wheel, and a lotus.
In the west is Amitābha, red, holding a red lotus, a sword, a jewel, and a wheel. In the north is Amoghasiddhi, green, holding a sword, a wheel, a jewel, and a lotus.
These three have black and white faces on their right and left [sides] respectively; all these Tathāgatas wear jeweled crowns and are adorned with various precious ornaments.
In the southeast is Locanā, equal to Vairocana;
in the southwest is Māmakī, equal to Akṣobhya, holding a red lotus, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus, because such is the reading in all the *sādhanas*.
In the northwest is Pāṇḍarā, equal to Amitābha;
in the northeast is Tārā, equal to Ratneśa, holding a yellow lotus, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
Outside this inner enclosure, in the southeast corner is Rūpavajrā, resembling Vairocana, holding a jewel-mirror, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
In the southwest is Śabdavajrā, equal to Akṣobhya, holding a blue lute, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus;
in the northwest is Gandhavajrā, equal to Ratneśa, yellow in color, holding a perfume conch, a sword, a wheel, and a lotus;
in the northeast is Rasavajrā, resembling Amitābha, red in color, holding a vessel of liquid, a sword, a jewel, and a wheel.
On the northern side of the eastern gate is Sparśavajrā, equal to Amoghasiddhi, holding a multicolored garment, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus;
on the southern side of the eastern gate is Dharmadhātuvajrā, equal to Vajrasattva, white in color, holding a source of phenomena (dharmodaya), a sword, a jewel, and a lotus.
These deities, beginning with Mañjuvajra, have three faces and six arms;
they hold the first two symbols with the two right hands and the other two with the two left hands.
In all cases, the root face has the same color as the body.
In the eastern and other gates are Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Amṛtakuṇḍali.
(AM 230) Here, Mañjuvajra, Vairocana, and the ten goddesses are seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon moons; the others are upon suns. Upon the discs of the moon and sun are double lotuses.
The Tathāgatas embrace their own wisdom-consorts with their two principal arms, while the goddesses embrace their own means.

As for the Lord of the Family (kulādhipati), Akṣobhya is the [presiding] Tathāgata Mañjuvajra and so forth on the head; Vairocana is [the presiding Tathāgata] for Locanā, Rūpavajrā, Yamāntaka, and the others; and Ratneśa is [the presiding Tathāgata] for Gandhavajrā. Furthermore, he is the [presiding Tathāgata] for the eight wrathful deities situated within the protection wheel.
Amitābha is the lord of Pāṇḍarā, Rasavajrā, and Padmāntaka; Amoghasiddhi is the lord of Tārā and Sparśavajrā;
and Vajradhara is the lord of Dharmadhātuvajrā.
Others say he is Akṣobhya.

Vajrasattva here has a white complexion tinged with a slight redness; his right and left faces are blue and red respectively. With his two principal arms he embraces his consort of his own nature; he holds a blue vajra, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus. He is seated upon a moon on a double lotus, possesses moon-like radiance, and sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
He wears a jeweled crown, is adorned with jewel ornaments, and is marked by Akṣobhya.

Here, within the chest of Mañjuvajra, there is a wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) resembling the pledge-being (*samayasattva*); in the moon at his heart is the seed-syllable *maṃ*, situated upon a moon and the hilt of a sword.
In the hearts of the symbols of Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya, there are, as appropriate, on a moon or a sun, the syllables *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*.
For the goddesses beginning with Locanā, they are *loṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*, *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*, *khaṃ*, and *raṃ*.
HŪṂ for the wrathful deities;
the heart-mantras of all the deities are stated in the *Vajrāvalī*.
(231a) Here, for the perfected yogin, the consecration of the eyes and so forth, as well as the entry of the gnosis-being and so on, have not been mentioned.

Even without that [the aforementioned process], because of the firmness of repeated mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*), the desired deity— whose form is delightful with a multitude of qualities such as the immeasurable and inconceivable superknowledge of the eye— is perfected in all its aspects in an utterly pure state in a single moment;
however, the mention of the heart-mantra and so forth is for the purpose of application in rites such as the consecration of the flask (*kalaśādhivāsana*).
But when another Tathāgata, the Leader, is in the center, then one situated in the middle should stand in his place;
for although Amitābha is white, it is said here that "the qualities (dharmas) are white by nature," and thus Vāgīśa is white.

Furthermore, regarding the mandalas to be described here, whichever deity of that mandala is said to occupy the primary position, she alone is the principal one facing the Lord of the Mandala (*maṇḍaleśa*).
However, when she is embraced by him, she faces him alone, because she has moved to his other side.

In this context, there are three peripheral elements surrounding the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*): the vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*), the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*), and the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*).
Among these, we shall explain that while the vajra-fence serves as the protection wheel for all the peaked pavilions to be described hereafter, the source of phenomena belongs only to some.

Regarding the houses of written symbols (lekhya-kūṭāgāra), it is stated in the *Vajrāvalī* that they are drawings indicating either the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) whose nature is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), or that which is contained within the realm of phenomena.

Just as it is externally, so it is internally; thus, by way of demonstrating the maṇḍala of the generation stage, the drawing of the vajra-fence—which indicates the rim of the world-system—is necessarily performed. The protection wheel is not drawn in this manner, and therefore it is not drawn here;
however, the warding off of obstacles is accomplished in another way.

Furthermore, since the Blessed Lady Śūnyatā alone is capable of uprooting the entire flood of obstacles along with their very foundations, it was not described as being drawn in the written maṇḍalas; rather, the drawing of the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) was intended solely to generate reverence for the firmness of conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in her.
As for the meditated maṇḍalas, however, its visualization is mentioned only in certain instances, and not in all.

Since the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) does not exist even in the meditated mandala because one enters into emptiness immediately after the destruction of obstacles, it is therefore not drawn here.
If that is so, then the vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*), which indicates the Cakravāḍa mountain range, should likewise not be drawn.
Now, regarding the arising of the gabled palace (*kūṭāgāra*)...
That [vajra-fence] arises;
for nowhere has the Blessed One stated that there is a second arising of the vajra-fence.
Or what is the use of generating it twice?

For once it has been generated, the vajra-ground, bonds, walls, and so forth, which are illusory in nature and have emptiness as their essence—being free from all superimpositions—remain exactly as they are.
Even though the protection wheel exists, its non-drawing within the mandalas has already been explained.
However, some authorities also approve of drawing a protection wheel in certain instances.
Thus ends the Mañjuvajra mandala.
